learningObjective: Compare compute and memory patterns of RMSNorm vs LayerNorm and identify which reduction operations each requires.

canonicalClaims.claim: RMSNorm requires exactly one reduction (E[x^2]) and no mean subtraction; LayerNorm requires two moments (E[x] and E[x^2]) which can be gathered in a single reduction pass and includes a mean-subtract and bias add per element.
conditions: Row fits in one program's on-chip working set for single-pass implementation.
Both are per-row (last-axis) normalizations on the same input shape.
nonImplications: Does not imply RMSNorm and LayerNorm are numerically equivalent.
Does not imply RMSNorm always yields measurable wall-clock speedup; both are memory-bound.

misconceptions.claim: RMSNorm requires computing the mean of x.
misconceptions.whyWrong: RMSNorm uses only mean(x^2); the mean of x is not part of the formula.

misconceptions.claim: LayerNorm needs two separate passes over x to gather mean and variance.
misconceptions.whyWrong: One pass accumulating both sum and sum-of-squares (or Welford) suffices.

misconceptions.claim: RMSNorm and LayerNorm have identical per-element compute cost.
misconceptions.whyWrong: RMSNorm skips (x - mean) subtraction and often the bias add; per-element ops are slightly fewer.

implementationFacts: Modern LLMs (Llama, Mistral) adopt RMSNorm for slight efficiency gains and empirical training stability.
Both are typically fused with the following linear op's input read to save HBM traffic.
performanceScenarios: Both are memory-bound; runtime is dominated by streaming x once and writing y once.
